profile.aboutMe:
I am a fourth-year Bachelor of Science in Information Technology student at Datamex College of Saint Adeline. I am building practical experience in web development, databases, data analysis, desktop application development, and IT problem-solving. My projects include Joshua's Studio House Museum, a front-end art gallery and storefront presentation demo with artwork collections, product variants, a browser-local cart, and simulated commission requests. It is designed for presentation only and does not accept real orders or payments. TechZone Mobile Store uses Python, Streamlit, Excel, SQL, and data visualizations to compare smartphone products and support inventory screening. I am also developing Buo, a local-first Python/Kivy fitness application focused on strength logging, training plans, recovery check-ins, reminders, analytics, and private progress tracking. A Windows desktop run setup is included; GPS route capture and Android-specific tracking remain incomplete.

I approach technical work by understanding the problem, breaking it into manageable tasks, testing what I build, and documenting results and limitations. I value continuous learning, responsible handling of information, clear communication, and evidence-based decisions. My current career direction is entry-level IT support and technical support, while continuing to strengthen my development and data skills. I want to contribute to a team, help users solve technology problems, and grow into a dependable IT professional. This portfolio presents my current work honestly: completed deliverables, working prototypes, and areas that still need testing or improvement.

troubleshooting.title: GitHub Pages cannot run server-side portfolio features
troubleshooting.status: Platform limitation confirmed · static edition prepared · public deployment pending
troubleshooting.problem: The original portfolio used server-dependent pages for editing content, saving contact messages, and managing uploaded evidence. GitHub Pages cannot execute server-side application code, so those features would not work when deployed there.
troubleshooting.possibleCauses: The selected hosting platform serves static HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and other static assets. It does not provide a server runtime or shared relational database for this website.
troubleshooting.diagnosticProcedure: Reviewed the deployment target requirements and the portfolio source structure. Identified server-side routes and database-dependent features, then separated the content and public pages from those backend components.
troubleshooting.solution: Prepared a separate static edition using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and JSON-based content. Project case studies and the defense presentation now render in the browser. Contact uses email/social links, and documentation explains how to edit content and publish updates through GitHub.
troubleshooting.lessonLearned: Choose a hosting platform based on the application runtime. A static hosting service is appropriate for a static portfolio, but server-side editing, uploads, and stored messages require a separate backend.

troubleshooting.title: TechZone source CSV contains appended summary rows
troubleshooting.problem: The original TechZone CSV has 29 data rows after the header, but only 15 rows represent actual smartphone products. Fourteen appended summary rows have blank Model values and should not be treated as individual phones.
troubleshooting.possibleCauses: Summary labels and aggregate values were appended to the raw file; treating every row as a product would inflate counts and distort statistics.
troubleshooting.diagnosticProcedure: Inspect the Model column; count rows with valid product model names; compare the data structure with the assignment’s expected 15 products; and check missing values and duplicate Brand–Model pairs after filtering.
troubleshooting.solution: Keep the 15 actual smartphone records and exclude the 14 appended summary rows from product-level calculations. The cleaned dataset reports 15 valid records, 10 brands, no missing required product fields, and no duplicate Brand–Model pairs.
troubleshooting.lessonLearned: Data cleaning starts with understanding what each row represents. Summary rows must not be mixed with individual observations during descriptive analysis.

troubleshooting.title: Buo GPS route capture is not implemented in the supplied snapshot
troubleshooting.problem: The app exposes activity and route-related screens/helpers, but GPS start/stop and location callbacks are stubs. Route distance, browser-map, and GPX helper functions return placeholder values.
troubleshooting.possibleCauses: The supplied build prioritizes local strength training and retains route-related UI or legacy data structures without a completed location-capture implementation.
troubleshooting.diagnosticProcedure: Inspect BuoApp.start_gps_tracking, stop_gps_tracking, on_gps_status, and on_gps_location, then check route helper functions such as haversine_km, build_static_map_url, build_route_browser_url, and build_gpx. Test location permissions and callbacks only after implementing them.
troubleshooting.solution: No GPS fix is claimed. Keep the portfolio description explicit that GPS route capture is incomplete. Implement permission checks, location callbacks, distance calculation, route persistence, and tests before presenting the feature as operational.
troubleshooting.lessonLearned: A route screen or Android permission declaration does not prove that GPS tracking is implemented. Verify callbacks and stored location results on a real device.

troubleshooting.title: Buo app-side background tracking does not start
troubleshooting.problem: The package contains service/background_tracker.py and a Buildozer service declaration, but BuoApp.start_background_tracking returns False and does not start the declared service.
troubleshooting.possibleCauses: The service script and Buildozer declaration were supplied as a foundation, while the application-side lifecycle and service start/stop bridge has not been implemented.
troubleshooting.diagnosticProcedure: Inspect BuoApp.start_background_tracking and stop_background_tracking, check the service declaration path in buildozer.spec, build a debug APK, and collect Android logcat output while testing service start, stop, notification, and process lifecycle.
troubleshooting.solution: No working background service is claimed. Connect the app lifecycle to the Android service API, handle permissions and foreground notifications, then verify behavior on supported Android versions and device manufacturers.
troubleshooting.lessonLearned: A service script existing in the repository does not mean the application starts it. Confirm the complete lifecycle from the UI action through Android service execution.

securityCase.title: Cybersecurity Case Study — SQL Injection
securityCase.vulnerability: SQL injection occurs when an application builds a database query in a way that allows untrusted input to change the intended SQL command.
securityCase.howItHappens: A common cause is concatenating form input directly into an SQL statement. An attacker may then supply input that changes the query logic. This case is for defensive understanding and authorized testing only.
securityCase.risks: Depending on the query and database permissions, SQL injection may expose records, bypass an authentication check, alter data, or damage data. The actual impact depends on the application and account privileges.
securityCase.prevention: Use parameterized queries supported by the chosen database library; keep untrusted input separate from SQL structure; validate application rules on the server; and avoid building SQL by concatenating raw input.
securityCase.practices: Use least-privilege database accounts where a database is required, protect configuration files and credentials, avoid showing raw database errors to visitors, keep software updated, back up important data, and test only systems for which you have permission.
securityCase.demonstration: Show a safe, language-neutral comparison between a vulnerable string-concatenated query and a parameterized query using harmless sample input. Do not test a real third-party website or publish database credentials.

interviews.answer: Prepare a genuine example. A strong structure is to list deliverables, divide work into small tasks, prioritize required features, set checkpoints, test early, and communicate risks before the deadline.

interviews.question: How do you work with a team?
interviews.answer: Use a real school or workplace example. Explain your assigned responsibility, how you shared updates, how you handled a disagreement or delay, and how you supported the overall result.

interviews.question: Why should an organization consider hiring you?
interviews.answer: Connect your practical project experience, willingness to learn, step-by-step troubleshooting approach, and ability to explain technical work. Support each claim with a specific example.

interviews.question: What technology are you currently learning?
interviews.answer: A current example is Python/Kivy desktop application development through Buo. Explain the Python package structure, local SQLite data layer, Windows desktop setup, and the screens you have actually tested. Distinguish desktop features from Android-specific GPS, sensors, and background services that remain incomplete.

interviews.question: Where do you want to develop professionally?
interviews.answer: Explain your current interest in entry-level IT support or technical support, then describe how you plan to strengthen Windows, networking, troubleshooting, user communication, secure application practices, and practical testing.

reflection.text:
My experience in the Bachelor of Science in Information Technology program has helped me understand that working in IT is not only about writing code or using software. It also involves understanding a problem, choosing an appropriate solution, checking whether that solution works, and explaining the result to other people. Before and during my studies, I was still developing my technical foundation. Through school activities and personal projects, I have become more familiar with web development, databases, data analysis, and mobile application development. I also learned that I need patience and a step-by-step approach when troubleshooting unfamiliar errors.

One important part of my learning has been developing the presentation version of Joshua's Studio House Museum, a web-based art gallery and storefront. The static demo brings together curated Graphite, Canvas, and Artisan Artifacts collections, product variants, a browser-local cart, and simulated commission requests. I worked with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS, and browser localStorage. I intentionally removed the payment and backend requirements from this presentation version because it is intended to demonstrate the interface and user flow, not accept real orders. This taught me to distinguish a front-end prototype from a production e-commerce system and to label its limitations clearly.

TechZone Mobile Store strengthened my understanding of data analysis. I worked with a smartphone dataset and learned to clean the source records before calculating statistics. The original file contained appended summary rows, so the analysis retained the 15 actual smartphone records rather than treating those summary rows as products. The project brought together Python, Pandas, NumPy, Streamlit, Excel, SQL, and visualizations. I learned to explain averages, compare brands, examine price and rating relationships, and turn findings into cautious recommendations. An important lesson was to state what the data cannot prove: the dataset contains product specifications, prices, and ratings, but it does not contain real transactions or sales history. Therefore, the system supports product comparison and inventory screening, not sales forecasting.

My specialization project is Buo, a local-first fitness and strength-progress application built with Python and Kivy. The supplied source includes a local SQLite data layer, strength logging, training plans, workout timers, recovery check-ins, reminders, a private journal, analytics, and export functions. I prepared a Windows desktop setup so it can be demonstrated in its own application window without requiring an Android APK. The desktop dependencies and launcher scripts are included, and I have confirmed that the application opens on my Windows computer. I also confirmed a successful online Gemini response, while other individual tools still need additional testing. GPS route capture and the app-side Android background-tracking launcher remain incomplete, and Android-specific sensor features are outside the current desktop presentation scope.

I have also encountered practical troubleshooting situations while choosing how to publish my portfolio. I learned that GitHub Pages is designed for static websites and cannot run server-side application features, so I prepared a separate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript edition that can be hosted without a paid PHP server or database. Reviewing Buo's package imports reinforced the importance of consistent filenames and module references. These examples taught me to gather evidence before changing configuration.

I used AI tools as learning and development support for organizing requirements, understanding code, and preparing documentation. I still need to review AI-generated suggestions carefully, compare them with source files, and test important behavior myself. AI can make mistakes, misread a project, or suggest features that are not actually implemented. I should never publish passwords, API keys, private records, or other sensitive information when asking for technical help.

I know that I still have areas to improve, particularly structured troubleshooting, networking fundamentals, secure web development, desktop runtime testing, secure deployment, and professional documentation. My immediate goal is to finish verifying my projects, organize their source code and evidence, and prepare a clear resume and portfolio. I am interested in beginning in IT support or technical support, where I can help users, learn from experienced colleagues, and develop strong operational skills. Over time, I also want to continue building software and data-related solutions. I consider myself ready to begin growing professionally because I have practical projects to discuss, a willingness to learn, and a better understanding of why testing, honesty, and continuous improvement matter in IT.
